nodes.description: Three of the numbered CVID subtypes disable the same structure: the B-cell coreceptor complex of CD19, CD21 (CR2), CD81 and CD225, which lowers the activation threshold of the B-cell antigen receptor. CD19 carries the signalling function, CD81 is required for CD19 to reach the surface, and CD21 supplies the C3d costimulus. MS4A1 (CD20) is not a subunit of that complex; it is grouped on this node because ClinGen's assessment records that CD20 regulates signalling through the B-cell receptor, and because the reported patient's defect was in antibody formation rather than in B-cell development. Across these subtypes B-cell development is largely preserved and what fails is the response to antigen, which is why they present as CVID rather than as agammaglobulinemia.

nodes.description: The hallmark of CVID is a failure of B cells to differentiate into immunoglobulin-secreting plasma cells. Defective class-switch recombination leads to impaired production of IgG, IgA, and often IgM. Most patients show reduced switched memory B cells (CD27+IgD-IgM-). Defects in B cell receptor signaling, BAFF/APRIL axis, and NF-kB signaling all converge on impaired germinal center output.

nodes.description: A lesion upstream of, and distinct from, the germinal-centre failure the node above describes. IKAROS is a lymphoid transcription factor, and the six reported mutations all fall in its DNA-binding domain, producing a progressive loss of circulating B cells with markedly reduced early B-cell precursors in marrow. Plasma cells were still present in the marrow of the reported patients, which is why this is modelled as its own node rather than added to the differentiation-and-class-switch node: the hypogammaglobulinemia follows from having too few B cells rather than from B cells that cannot finish differentiating.

nodes.description: CVID-associated granulomatous and lymphocytic interstitial lung disease (GLILD) involves poorly organized granulomas with abundant T and B cells. Moreover, B-cell abnormalities are prominent in CVID, with elevated IgM, BAFF, and CD21low B cells correlating with granulomatous disease progression.

nodes.description: Approximately 25-50% of CVID patients develop autoimmune complications, most commonly autoimmune cytopenias (immune thrombocytopenia and autoimmune hemolytic anemia). This reflects a breakdown of peripheral tolerance and defective regulatory T cell function, particularly through the CTLA-4/LRBA checkpoint axis. Expansion of autoreactive CD21low B cells contributes to antibody-mediated autoimmunity. IKZF1 (IKAROS) is bound here as a second placement, not as its primary mechanism: its CVID lesion is the loss of the B-cell compartment modelled on the Early B Cell Lymphopoiesis Failure node, and it appears again here because autoimmune cytopenias are a recurrent part of the IKAROS phenotype rather than an incidental feature of one case.

nodes.description: Two CVID subtypes sit on the two arms of NF-kB signalling. NFKB1 haploinsufficiency reduces the canonical p50 subunit and is reported as the commonest monogenic cause of CVID in Europeans; NFKB2 C-terminal truncating variants leave the non-canonical precursor p100 unprocessable, so the mature p52 subunit is not made. The two are grouped on one node because both converge on impaired B-cell differentiation, and separated in the bound processes because the pathways themselves are distinct.

nodes.description: Many CVID patients exhibit T cell abnormalities including reduced naive CD4+ T cells, expanded CD21low B cells, impaired T cell proliferation, and skewed T helper cell responses. T follicular helper cell dysfunction contributes to impaired germinal center reactions and defective B cell help. ICOS deficiency specifically impairs T cell help for late B cell differentiation and memory B cell generation. IL-21, a cytokine of the same follicular helper compartment, is grouped here for the same reason: its loss removes the T-cell-derived signal for B-cell differentiation rather than damaging the B cell itself.

evidence.snippet: we found four of 32 patients to lack ICOS, the "inducible costimulator" on activated T cells, due to an inherited homozygous deletion in the ICOS gene. T cells from these individuals were normal with regard to subset distribution, activation, cytokine production and proliferation. In contrast, naive, switched and memory B cells were reduced.
